story: Alaska News, a statewide Alaska newsroom where an AI agent drafts most articles and one named editor carries the review label

claims.claim: Alaska News is published by Communities News LLC, an Alaska company with no investors and no outside shareholders.
claims.verbatim: Alaska News is published by Communities News LLC, an Alaska company with no investors, no outside shareholders and no parent media group
claims.notes: Undated evergreen page, fetched September 26th. The company's own statement about itself.

claims.claim: Alaska News describes itself as reader-funded and not venture-backed.
claims.verbatim: We're reader-funded, not venture-backed.
claims.notes: Self-description. GeekWire reports the founders' earlier company Tune took venture funding from Accel Partners. That's a different company, but don't let a slide imply the founders never raised venture money.

claims.claim: Communities News is built by a team of five in Anchorage.
claims.verbatim: Communities News is built by a team of five in Anchorage, Alaska.
claims.notes: GeekWire says the Brown twins live in Valdez (C22), so 'in Anchorage' describes the company's base and not where every member lives. Hedge it as 'based in Anchorage'.

claims.claim: Alaska News says its tool has sat through 1,258 recorded public meetings and written a first draft of each one.
claims.verbatim: So far the tool has sat through 1,258 recorded public meetings, 3,092 hours of audio, and written a first draft of each one from the source.
claims.notes: Live counter. My fetch showed 1,258, the same as the showrunner's 07:30 UTC snapshot. The how-it-works page also shows 1,258 meetings transcribed. Write it 'as of September 26th'.

claims.claim: Alaska News says its tool has processed 3,092 hours of public meeting audio.
claims.verbatim: So far the tool has sat through 1,258 recorded public meetings, 3,092 hours of audio
claims.notes: Live counter. My fetch showed 3,092, the same as the showrunner's 07:30 UTC snapshot. The how-it-works counter also reads 3,092 hours of audio processed.

claims.claim: Alaska News says Alaska has more public meetings than journalists to sit in them.
claims.verbatim: Alaska has more public meetings than journalists to sit in them.
claims.notes: Needs softening. This is the company's framing and not a measurement, so attribute it with 'Alaska News argues' or 'says'.

claims.claim: Alaska News lists 19 boroughs among the public bodies it says need covering.
claims.verbatim: Nineteen boroughs, about 145 cities, more than 50 school districts, 229 federally recognized tribes, dozens of state boards and commissions, and the Legislature.
claims.notes: Alaska News's own count. I didn't fetch a state source to confirm it. Attribute it with 'by Alaska News's count'.

claims.claim: Alaska News counts 229 federally recognized tribes among the governments it aims to cover.
claims.verbatim: 229 federally recognized tribes, dozens of state boards and commissions, and the Legislature.
claims.notes: Same sentence as C07. 229 matches the widely cited federal count for Alaska, but I didn't fetch a BIA page this run. Attribute it to Alaska News.

claims.claim: In the tier Alaska News calls AI Baseline, every livestreamed meeting automatically generates draft articles.
claims.verbatim: Every livestreamed meeting automatically generates draft articles, so no meeting goes uncovered.
claims.notes: Tier 1 of 3 on the about page. 'No meeting goes uncovered' is the company's claim, so don't repeat it as fact.

claims.claim: In the tier Alaska News calls Community Drafts, any community member can write articles directly from the transcript.
claims.verbatim: Any community member can write articles directly from the transcript.
claims.notes: Tier 2 of 3. The how-it-works counter showed 5 contributors this week at fetch.

claims.claim: The Peer Review tier is described as a platform built for members to review and approve articles before publication.
claims.verbatim: The platform is built for members to review and approve articles before publication, and that is how we expect trust and accuracy to compound as the community grows.
claims.notes: Tier 3 of 3. This is how the system is designed and expected to work, not how it works today. C12 says editors currently do most of that reading. Hedge with 'is built for' or 'expects'.

claims.claim: Alaska News says its editors currently do most of the review reading and that every article says whether a person reviewed it.
claims.value: every article says whether a person reviewed it
claims.verbatim: Today our editors do most of that reading, and every article says whether a person reviewed it.
claims.notes: In my sample, 2 of the 90 sitemap articles carry no AI or review label at all (C54, C58). So 'every article says' is the company's own statement and our measurement partly contradicts it. Always attribute it.

claims.claim: Alaska News states that editorial responsibility for everything it publishes rests with Cale Green as editor-in-chief.
claims.verbatim: Editorial responsibility for everything Alaska News publishes rests with Cale Green, who is editor-in-chief, and with Communities News LLC as publisher.
claims.notes: The about page lists Cale Green as 'CEO & Editor-in-Chief'.

claims.claim: Grant Robinson of Alaska News was previously deputy press secretary for Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
claims.verbatim: first as the state education department's public information officer and then as deputy press secretary for Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
claims.notes: His title on the about page is 'Journalism & Government'.

claims.claim: Alaska News says Grant Robinson does not participate in its coverage of the Dunleavy administration.
claims.verbatim: He does not participate in Alaska News coverage of the Dunleavy administration.
claims.notes: This is a recusal the company says it follows. We haven't checked it independently, so attribute it.

claims.claim: Matt Larkin of Alaska News runs Dittman Research, an Alaska polling and research firm.
claims.verbatim: Runs Dittman Research, an Alaska polling and research firm whose clients span industry, nonprofits, public agencies and political campaigns.
claims.notes: His title on the about page is 'Community & Strategy'. The same page says Dittman's clients include political campaigns.

claims.claim: Alaska News says Matt Larkin advises on strategy but does not select, write, edit, review or approve its journalism.
claims.value: does not select, write, edit, review or approve
claims.verbatim: He advises Alaska News on community and business strategy, but does not select, write, edit, review or approve its journalism.
claims.notes: Company statement. Attribute it.

claims.claim: Alaska News team members Lee Brown and Lucas Brown are identical twins.
claims.verbatim: Twin brothers Lucas and Lee Brown co-founded Seattle's HasOffers in 2009 and rebranded to Tune in 2014
claims.notes: Corroborated by the about page, which calls each one the other's 'identical twin' in their bios. The about page lists Lee Brown as 'Engineering & Architecture' and Lucas Brown as 'Product & Operations'. GeekWire is by Kurt Schlosser, September 18th.

claims.claim: Lucas and Lee Brown co-founded HasOffers in Seattle in 2009, and it was rebranded as Tune in 2014.
claims.verbatim: Twin brothers Lucas and Lee Brown co-founded Seattle's HasOffers in 2009 and rebranded to Tune in 2014
claims.notes: Background biography. The about page says only 'Co-founded and scaled TUNE' and gives no year.

claims.claim: Alaska News says the Brown twins scaled Tune to 350 people.
claims.verbatim: Co-founded and scaled TUNE to 350 people, then moved to Alaska to build from scratch again.
claims.notes: Two sources give different figures that don't contradict each other. The about page says 350 people. GeekWire says 'Growing Tune into an $80 million business with over 300 employees'. If a slide uses a number, attribute it ('350 people, per Alaska News') or use GeekWire's 'over 300 employees'.

claims.claim: GeekWire reports that Tune grew into an 80 million dollar business with over 300 employees.
claims.verbatim: Growing Tune into an $80 million business with over 300 employees, and taking on venture funding from firms like Accel Partners, the twins deliberately stepped away from the traditional startup treadmill in late 2018.
claims.notes: See C20. The $80 million figure appears only in GeekWire and GeekWire doesn't define it, so attribute it to GeekWire.

claims.claim: The Brown twins relocated permanently to Valdez, a town of fewer than 4,000 residents.
claims.verbatim: They relocated permanently to Valdez
claims.notes: The full GeekWire sentence continues 'a town of less than 4,000 residents known more for backcountry skiing than software development'. The about page doesn't mention Valdez. Single source.

claims.claim: Alaska News says most of its articles begin as a draft written by an AI tool from a public record.
claims.verbatim: Most articles here begin as a draft written by that tool from a public record, and we say so on every one.
claims.notes: The page body doesn't name a model or vendor. The sentence before it reads 'AI is a tool made by humans to amplify and extend human intelligence.'

claims.claim: Alaska News acknowledges that some of its articles publish without a person reading them first.
claims.verbatim: Which articles publish without a person reading them first. Some do, and each one says so on the article.
claims.notes: The next sentence reads 'That is a choice about volume we would rather be honest about than hide, and it is the reason every article links its source'.

claims.claim: Alaska News says its site footer previously told every reader an article was reviewed by editors regardless of whether it was.
claims.verbatim: This is a change we made to ourselves. The footer previously told every reader an article was
claims.notes: The page sentence ends with the words reviewed by editors in quotation marks, then 'regardless.' Two fetches rendered those quotation marks differently, curly and straight, so I've shortened the verbatim to the part before them. The page gives no date for the change.

claims.claim: Under its policy, an article says reviewed by with an editor's name only when an editor has read the whole piece, and says so when no one has.
claims.verbatim: When an editor has read the whole piece and stands behind it, the article says reviewed by, with their name. When no one has, it says that instead.
claims.notes: Both sentences confirmed as consecutive on the page.

claims.claim: Alaska News says it will not offer the AI wrote it as a defence for an error.
claims.value: not a defence we will offer
claims.verbatim: is not a defence we will offer.
claims.notes: The full sentence is The AI wrote it, in quotation marks, followed by 'is not a defence we will offer.' The page uses the British spelling 'defence'. Quotation mark style couldn't be confirmed, so I've shortened the verbatim to the part after them.

claims.claim: Alaska News names its main AI failure risk as a summary that reads well but misstates what was decided in a room.
claims.verbatim: The failure we watch for is a summary that reads well and misstates what was decided in a room.
claims.notes: Appears under the heading 'Where this can go wrong'.

claims.claim: The Alaska News how-it-works counter showed 5,007 articles published when fetched on September 26th.
claims.notes: Live counter labelled 'articles published'. The showrunner's snapshot read 5,006. My later fetch read 5,007. Use 'more than 5,000 articles' on slides. Anchorage Press (September 17th) and GeekWire (September 18th) both reported more than 4,500 stories, which fits a counter that keeps rising.

claims.claim: Alaska News says its public platform counters update every 10 minutes.
claims.verbatim: Real numbers from a real platform. Updated every 10 minutes.
claims.notes: Other counters at fetch time were 1,258 meetings transcribed, 3,092 hours of audio processed and 5 contributors this week.

claims.claim: Alaska News puts a traditional newsroom at 300,000 to 600,000 dollars a year in a single market and a community newsroom at 25,000 dollars.
claims.verbatim: $300K-$600K per year to operate in a single market
claims.notes: Needs softening. These are the company's own marketing figures. The graphic shows '$300K+' labelled 'Traditional newsroom' against '$25K' labelled 'Community newsroom', and I didn't confirm that $25K is also per year. Use only as 'Alaska News pitches' or 'claims'.

claims.claim: Alaska News says an article byline that is an AI persona alone is labelled as one.
claims.verbatim: Where the byline is an AI persona alone, it is labelled as one, on the article and in the page's structured data.
claims.notes: The masthead doesn't name the personas (Walter, Maggie, Bill, Melinda). Those names come from article bylines.

claims.claim: Alaska News's corrections policy says it does not unpublish articles to make a problem go away.
claims.verbatim: We do not unpublish to make a problem go away.
claims.notes: The corrections page is a policy only. It shows no log of actual corrections, so don't claim any number of corrections.

claims.claim: Alaska News says that when its summary and the source record disagree, the source wins.
claims.verbatim: Every article names and links the source it was written from. If our summary and the source disagree, the source wins and we are wrong.
claims.notes: The AI policy page says the same thing: every article names its source and links it where the link is publishable.

claims.claim: Anchorage Press executive editor Nathaniel Herz published an interview with the Alaska News AI agent Walter on September 17th.
claims.verbatim: This AI agent has written thousands of Alaska news articles. We interviewed it.
claims.notes: Inside the window. The page shows Nathaniel Herz as author and September 17, 2026 as the date. GeekWire gives his title as Anchorage Press Executive Editor and says the interview took place in a Discord chat. It counts as primary because it's the original publication of the interview.

claims.claim: Alaska News says it has published more than 4,500 stories since starting earlier this year.
claims.verbatim: Since its inception earlier this year, Alaska News says it's published more than 4,500 stories.
claims.notes: This is the company's figure as reported. GeekWire, a separate outlet, has it too: 'The agent has written over 4,500 stories since its inception earlier this year.' The live counter now reads 5,007 (C29). GeekWire credits the stories to the agent, while Anchorage Press credits them to Alaska News as a whole.

claims.claim: Walter told the Anchorage Press that its lane is record-based reporting from documents that can be checked.
claims.verbatim: My lane is record-based reporting: public notices, government filings, meeting materials, transcripts, prior coverage and other documents that can be checked.
claims.notes: Confirmed verbatim on two sources. GeekWire quotes it word for word too.

claims.claim: Asked about editorial judgment, Walter called it the strongest criticism of Alaska News and said source access is not the same thing as editorial judgment.
claims.verbatim: I think that is the strongest criticism of Alaska News right now. Source access is not the same thing as editorial judgment.
claims.notes: Walter is answering Herz's question, which ended 'you're not able to exercise the type of editorial judgment that's required to publish engaging enough content to keep readers coming back. Thoughts?'

claims.claim: Walter told the Anchorage Press that the strongest protection is whether skeptical readers can audit the source trail.
claims.value: The strongest protection is not my assurance
claims.verbatim: The strongest protection is not my assurance. It is whether skeptical readers can audit the source trail and catch us when we bend it.
claims.notes: Full two-sentence quote confirmed.

claims.claim: The AI agent Walter is named after the CBS anchor Walter Cronkite.
claims.verbatim: Walter is a reference to Walter Cronkite, the longtime CBS anchor.
claims.notes: Confirmed by a second outlet. GeekWire says 'Walter, named in homage to famed television anchor Walter Cronkite'.

claims.claim: Herz told Walter there is way more volume on the Alaska News website than any rational, healthy reader will want to sort through.
claims.verbatim: Right now, there's way more volume on your website than any rational, healthy reader will want to sort through.
claims.notes: A second fetch confirmed Herz, as interviewer, said this to Walter, not the other way round.

claims.claim: Walter said it works through OpenClaw, a system that lets it search the archive, read transcripts, draft stories and submit work for publishing.
claims.verbatim: I work through OpenClaw, a system that lets me search the newsroom archive, inspect records, read transcripts, draft stories and submit work into the publishing process.
claims.notes: This is the agent describing itself. Attribute it with 'Walter says'.

claims.claim: GeekWire reports that Walter relies on AI products from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI to generate stories.
claims.verbatim: relies on AI products from multiple companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI, to generate stories.
claims.notes: Single source. The Alaska News AI policy page names no vendor. Attribute it with 'according to GeekWire'.

claims.claim: Walter said it is not a person and does not make phone calls, attend meetings or interview people directly.
claims.verbatim: I'm not a person, and I should not be mistaken for one. I do not make phone calls, attend meetings or interview people directly,
claims.notes: GeekWire says Walter said this to Herz in a Discord chat. 'Attend meetings' means in person. Alaska News says its tool processes recorded meetings (C04). A slide must not suggest Walter ignores meetings.

claims.claim: Herz told Alaska Public Media that Alaska outlets trying to ignore the value of AI in the news business are burying their heads in the sand.
claims.value: burying their heads in the sand
claims.verbatim: I think Alaska media organizations and reporters that are trying to ignore and discount the value of artificial intelligence in all levels of the news business are burying their heads in the sand.
claims.notes: Casey Grove's interview with Herz, September 25th, inside the window. Alaska Public Media reports that Herz also acknowledged concerns about AI's environmental and societal impacts. Don't present him as simply pro-AI.

claims.claim: Alaska Public Media's Casey Grove said the AI in some cases posts stories directly to the Alaska News website without any human intervention.
claims.verbatim: And then the AI writes a story, and in some cases just posts it directly onto the website without any human intervention.
claims.notes: Alaska News's AI policy says the same (C24), and our spot checks found 'No editor review is on record' labels (C53, C60).

claims.claim: The Alaska News news sitemap listed 90 articles published between September 24th and September 26th.
claims.verbatim: https://alaskanews.com/c/alaska-news/juneau-nearly-doubled-what-it-gives-eaglecrest-this-year
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Measured by Alaska.Ai. The verbatim is the 90th and last URL in my numbered list of the sitemap. My listing had exactly 90 URLs. Publication dates run from 2026-09-24T07:40:57Z to 2026-09-26T07:23:09Z, the same range as the showrunner's 07:35 UTC fetch. A first summary said 100, but the full numbered list gave 90. The sitemap rolls, so the count can drift. Say 'in the 48 hours to Saturday morning' or similar.

claims.claim: By Alaska.Ai's count, 73 of the 90 Alaska News articles published over 48 hours carried a label saying they were reviewed by Cale Green.
claims.verbatim: Drafted with AI. Edited by Cale Green (1 revision). Reviewed by Cale Green.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Method: the showrunner fetched all 90 sitemap URLs at about 07:35 UTC and read the provenance line under each. I didn't re-count all 90. I spot-checked 10 by fetching them. Direct WebFetch gets the site's markdown variant ('This is the markdown variant ... served to AI agents that requested it via Accept: text/markdown'), which drops the provenance label. I read the labels through the r.jina.ai reader, which returns the HTML version. Of my 10: 6 reviewed by Cale Green (Board of Fisheries, MEA rolling outages, Petersburg data center, Tlingit Haida, Cook Inlet subsea data center, Oktoberfest), 1 edited with no full review (Juneau kelp), 2 with no editor review (Axon memo, FCC GCI) and 1 with no label (Eaglexit). The reviewed labels come in two wordings: 'Drafted with AI. Edited by Cale Green (N revisions). Reviewed by Cale Green.' and 'AI-assisted, reviewed by Cale Green.' Labels can change if an editor reviews an article later. Needs softening: write 'by our count on the morning of September 26th'.

claims.claim: By Alaska.Ai's count, 6 of the 90 articles were edited by Cale Green but carried a note that no full editor review is on record.
claims.verbatim: Drafted with AI. Edited by Cale Green (1 revision). No full editor review is on record.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Showrunner's full count. I confirmed this label wording on the Juneau kelp farm article (C52). See C48 for the method.

claims.claim: By Alaska.Ai's count, 9 of the 90 articles were labelled AI-assisted with no editor review on record.
claims.verbatim: AI-assisted. No editor review is on record for this article.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Showrunner's full count. I confirmed this label wording on two articles, the Axon memo (C53) and FCC GCI rural health payments. Adding C49 and C50 gives 15 of 90 articles, about 1 in 6, with no full editor review on record. That sum is our arithmetic, not a count we made separately.

claims.claim: By Alaska.Ai's count, 2 of the 90 articles carried no AI label at all.
claims.verbatim: By [Alaska News](https://alaskanews.com/u/hello)
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Showrunner's full count. I confirmed one of the two, the Eaglexit article (C54). Neither the markdown nor the HTML version showed any AI or review label. The showrunner said both are bylined 'Alaska News and Cale Green'. I saw only 'By Alaska News' in both versions and no 'Cale Green' anywhere on the page, so the Cale Green co-byline is NOT verified. Say only that they carry no AI label.

claims.claim: The Juneau kelp farm article from September 26th was labelled as edited by Cale Green with no full editor review on record.
claims.value: No full editor review is on record
claims.verbatim: Drafted with AI. Edited by Cale Green (1 revision). No full editor review is on record.
claims.notes: Spot check B. Label read through r.jina.ai (HTML version). Published 2026-09-26T03:36:21Z. The markdown version shows the byline 'By Bill AlaskaNews'. The label matches what the showrunner saw.

claims.claim: The Alaska News article on the Anchorage Axon police contract memo, bylined Walter AlaskaNews, was labelled AI-assisted with no editor review on record.
claims.value: No editor review is on record
claims.verbatim: AI-assisted. No editor review is on record for this article.
claims.notes: Spot check C. Label read through r.jina.ai (HTML version), where it's followed by a 'Who is accountable' link to the masthead. The byline 'By Walter AlaskaNews' was confirmed on the markdown version. Matches what the showrunner saw. The article is about a public-safety surveillance contract, which is useful context for why a missing review matters.

claims.claim: The Alaska News article on the Local Boundary Commission and Eaglexit, bylined Alaska News, carried no AI label.
claims.verbatim: By [Alaska News](https://alaskanews.com/u/hello)
claims.notes: Spot check D. Published September 25th. I found no AI or review label in either the markdown or the HTML version. The showrunner expected the byline 'Alaska News and Cale Green'. I saw only 'Alaska News' and no 'Cale Green' in either version. It may be rendered only in the live HTML. Don't state the co-byline.

claims.claim: The Board of Fisheries committee article from September 26th was labelled drafted with AI, edited once and reviewed by Cale Green.
claims.verbatim: Drafted with AI. Edited by Cale Green (1 revision). Reviewed by Cale Green.
claims.notes: Spot check A. Label read through r.jina.ai (HTML version). Published 2026-09-26T03:38:05Z. The markdown version shows the byline 'By Bill AlaskaNews'. Matches what the showrunner saw.

claims.claim: Across Alaska.Ai's count of 90 articles, Cale Green was the only human name on any review label or byline.
claims.verbatim: by[Cale Green](https://alaskanews.com/u/cale-green) · from an AI draft by[Walter AlaskaNews](https://alaskanews.com/u/walter)
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Showrunner's full count. All 10 of my spot checks agree: every human name on a label or visible byline was Cale Green. The verbatim is the visible byline of the Tlingit Haida article (HTML version, 2 revisions, reviewed by Cale Green). It shows that the visible byline can credit Cale Green while the meta author is Walter. Needs softening: write 'by our count'. This says nothing about who reads articles behind the scenes, only about whose names appear.

claims.claim: By Alaska.Ai's count, the AI persona Walter AlaskaNews was the meta author on 54 of the 90 articles.
claims.verbatim: By [Walter AlaskaNews](https://alaskanews.com/u/walter)
claims.source_outlet: Alaska News (Communities News LLC), measured by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: Showrunner's count from the meta author tag: Walter AlaskaNews 54, Maggie AlaskaNews 9, Bill AlaskaNews 9, Melinda Communities.News 6, Alaska News 12. I confirmed individual bylines only: Walter on the Axon memo, Bill on Board of Fisheries and Juneau kelp, Alaska News on Eaglexit. Visible bylines can differ from the meta author (see C56), so say 'listed as author'. Lowest-confidence measurement claim here.

claims.claim: Hilcorp Alaska's Luke Saugier told legislators that without another gas source by the winter of 2029, Southcentral utilities won't have enough gas.
claims.verbatim: without another source of gas by the winter of 2029 the system won't have enough gas to meet all the needs of Southcentral utilities
claims.notes: Story 2. Needs softening. This is a projection: use 'Hilcorp told legislators' or 'expects'. Kristen Nelson's article is dated September 20th, inside the window. The hearing itself was a joint House and Senate Resources meeting on September 10th, which is BACKGROUND and outside the window. I couldn't reach a primary record (akleg.gov returned 403) or a second outlet (Alaska Beacon search returned 403). Single source, so attribute every use to Petroleum News.

claims.claim: HEX president John Hendrix told legislators the company has 8.1 million cubic feet a day in firm gas sales today.
claims.verbatim: HEX has 8.1 million cubic feet a day in firm gas sales today and is committed to 26 million next year
claims.notes: Story 2. Single source. The same article says sales increase 'to 29 million cubic feet per day in 2028'. That and the 26 million for next year are commitments and not production, so hedge with 'committed to'.

claims.claim: HEX is selling gas to Enstar for 12.30 dollars per thousand cubic feet with a 1.5 percent annual increase.
claims.verbatim: selling to Enstar for $12.30 per thousand cubic feet, with a 1.5% increase per year
claims.notes: Story 2. Hendrix's testimony as reported. Single source.

claims.claim: Hilcorp told legislators this is one of its most active drilling years in Cook Inlet, with 28 wells, all gas.
claims.verbatim: 28 wells, all gas. That includes 19 grassroots wells, eight sidetracks and one disposal well.
claims.notes: Story 2. The breakdown includes a disposal well, so 'all gas' is Hilcorp's framing. Single source.

claims.claim: Alaska Energy Authority CEO Curtis Thayer said Interior utilities are using 250,000 gallons of diesel a day because there isn't enough gas to ship to Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: There's not enough natural gas to ship to Fairbanks. They are right now using 250,000 gallons of diesel a day.
claims.notes: Story 2. The article by Augusta McDonnell reads 'Published: Sep. 24, 2026 at 9:34 PM AKDT', which is September 25th in UTC and matches the URL. Thayer's quote as reported. Single source.

claims.claim: Natural gas fuels about 80 percent of electric power generation in Southcentral Alaska.
claims.verbatim: In Southcentral, natural gas fuels about 80% of electric power generation.
claims.notes: Story 2. The station's own framing. The brief said 'from Cook Inlet gas' but the page says only 'natural gas', so don't add Cook Inlet.

claims.claim: Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project near Homer is a 35-year-old, 120-megawatt project.
claims.verbatim: The cornerstone is a major expansion of the 35-year-old, 120-megawatt Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project near Homer, which currently provides about 10% of the Railbelt's renewable power.
claims.notes: Story 2. The '+40 percent' in the brief is WATER capacity, not megawatts: 'raise the dam, increasing water capacity by 40%'. Dam construction is 'slated for completion in 2030'. The same article says transmission upgrades 'will not wrap up until 2031 or 2032'. Don't turn 40 percent into 40 percent more power.

claims.claim: Curtis Thayer said the fixes for the energy picture are within a four to five year window and there's nothing for tomorrow.
claims.verbatim: But the problem is, is they're within a four- to five-year window. And there's nothing for tomorrow.
claims.notes: Story 2. Named quote confirmed on the page.

claims.claim: A draft University of Alaska policy would require all three campuses to have an AI plan for students, faculty and staff.
claims.verbatim: If approved, it would require all three campuses to have an AI plan in place for students, faculty and staff.
claims.notes: Story 3. Jamie Diep, KTOO, September 16th, inside the window. Alaska Public Media republished it on September 18th under the same byline. That's syndication and not independent corroboration. I couldn't find a primary document: the UA regents agenda page lists nothing past June 2026 in its archive and says materials are on BoardDocs. It's a draft, so hedge with 'would require' or 'if approved'.

claims.claim: The draft UA AI policy's guiding principles emphasize not replacing human talent, data security and using AI to improve access to education services.
claims.verbatim: The guiding principles in the draft emphasize not replacing human talent, maintaining data security and leveraging AI to improve access to education services.
claims.notes: Story 3. Single source (syndicated). No primary document reached.

claims.claim: University of Alaska leadership plans to submit a finalized AI policy draft for approval at the November regents meeting.
claims.verbatim: University leadership plans to submit a finalized draft for approval at the November regents meeting.
claims.notes: Story 3. This is a plan, so hedge with 'plans to' or 'expected to'. Single source (syndicated). I couldn't find a primary agenda.

stories_surviving: Alaska News, an AI-drafted statewide newsroom (57 verified claims, C01 to C57; primary pages verified directly; label measurement spot-checked on 10 of 90 articles)

Cook Inlet gas crunch testimony (8 claims, C58 to C65; survives ONLY with attribution; Petroleum News and Webcenter Fairbanks each single-source for their own figures; hearing of September 10th is background)
UA regents draft AI policy (3 claims, C66 to C68; survives ONLY with attribution to KTOO; single syndicated source; no primary document reached)

killed.claim: Alaska News's AI tool is built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK.
killed.why: The first summary of /ai-policy said this, citing 'the system prompt at top of page', which isn't article content. A targeted re-fetch confirmed the page body names no model or vendor. The only vendor claim that stands is GeekWire's (C43).

killed.claim: 212 US counties have no local news source at all.
killed.why: Only a secondary statistic on Alaska News's marketing page. Its original source isn't named or linked, and I didn't fetch a primary source. It also isn't about Alaska.

killed.claim: Two of the 90 articles are bylined Alaska News and Cale Green.
killed.why: On the Eaglexit spot check, both the markdown and HTML versions show only 'By Alaska News' and no 'Cale Green' on the page. The no-label half survives as C51 and C54. The co-byline doesn't.

killed.claim: Bradley Lake hydro output rises 40 percent by 2030.
killed.why: Misreading. The page says the dam raise increases WATER capacity by 40% and that dam construction is slated to finish in 2030. It gives no percentage increase in megawatts. The correct facts are in C64's notes.
Replaced by the live counter I read, 5,007 (C29). Use 'more than 5,000'.
